Series::argsort¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::argsort() const -> Series
Series::argsort(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::argsort(std::int64_t dim, bool descending) const -> Series
Series::argsort(std::int64_t dim, bool descending, bool stable) const -> Series

What It Does¶

argsort() returns an ordering plan rather than reordered values. Every output entry is an int64 position identifying which source entry should appear at that place in the sorted lane. The result has the same shape as the source, but its dtype is always int64.

This distinction is fundamental:

  • sort() answers “what are the values in order?”

  • argsort() answers “which source positions produce that order?”

The no-argument overload orders the final axis. An explicit dim chooses the axis whose local positions are returned. All other axes remain independent lanes. descending reverses the desired order; stable decides whether equal values retain their original relative order.

Overload Map¶

  • argsort() is ascending along the final axis.

  • argsort(dim) is ascending along dim.

  • argsort(dim, descending) chooses ascending or descending direction.

  • argsort(dim, descending, stable) also gives equal values a deterministic source-order policy when stable=true.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis that each returned index addresses. Positive dimensions count from the front; negative dimensions count from the end. The numbers in the output are local positions on this axis, not flattened addresses into the entire series.

descending (bool)

  • false: smallest values appear first.

  • true: largest values appear first.

It changes comparison direction only. The result remains an index series.

stable (bool)

  • true: if two values compare equal, their source order is preserved.

  • false: equal-value order is deliberately unspecified.

Use stable ordering when indices carry records, labels, or any other aligned meaning that must survive ties. Do not infer stability from a particular run when this toggle is false.

Returns¶

Series An int64 series whose shape matches the input. Applying those indices along the same axis yields the ordered values.

Gradient¶

argsort() creates control information, not a differentiable numeric value path. Treat its output as indices for a subsequent selection or reordering operation rather than as part of a reverse-mode objective.

Examples¶

Example 1. The default orders the final axis ascending.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, scores.argsort());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 3, 0, 2, 4]

Read this as scores[1], scores[3], scores[0], scores[2], scores[4], which are 1, 1, 3, 4, 5 in ascending order.

Example 2. Descending order reverses the plan.

std::cout << scores.argsort(0, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 2, 0, 1, 3]

Now the plan reads the values as 5, 4, 3, 1, 1.

Example 3. dim=0 orders each column independently, so the results are row positions.

auto table = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 1.0, 3.0}, {2.0, 5.0, 1.0}});
std::cout << table.argsort(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[1,2], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=false)
data=[[1, 0, 1],
  [0, 1, 0]]

For column 0, row 1 (2) comes before row 0 (4), so that column’s index lane is [1, 0].

Example 4. dim=1 instead returns column positions for each row.

std::cout << table.argsort(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 2, 0],
  [2, 0, 1]]

The same numeric index can therefore mean a row or a column position; dim defines that interpretation.

Example 5. Stable ordering makes equal-value provenance explicit.

auto tied = pluss::make_series({2LL, 1LL, 2LL, 1LL});
std::cout << tied.argsort(0, false, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 3, 0, 2]

The equal 1s retain source order 1, 3; the equal 2s retain 0, 2.

Example 6. Apply an ordering plan with index_select() to obtain the values.

auto order = scores.argsort();
std::cout << scores.index_select(0, order);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1, 3, 4, 5]

This separates discovery of the ordering from use of that ordering, which is useful when the same indices must reorder several aligned series.

Example 7. The selected dimension must exist.

try { std::cout << scores.argsort(1); }
catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cout << error.what(); }

Output¶

argsort: dim out of range

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • argsort() returns indices; streaming it does not show sorted values.

  • Indices are local to dim; they cannot be used as flat take() positions for a multi-dimensional source without changing their meaning.

  • Complex-valued inputs are rejected because this operation requires an order.

  • Equal values have a reliable relative-order guarantee only with stable=true.

Summary¶

Use argsort() when ordering itself is reusable information. Keep the result with the series it describes and apply it along the same axis to all aligned data that must be reordered consistently.
